title: The Middle Ages · Episode 4
chapters: Gothic cathedrals: how medieval builders made stone fly
Joan of Arc and the Hundred Years' War

units.t: The Middle Ages. Episode four.
In this episode: Magna Carta, Gothic cathedrals: how medieval builders made stone fly and Joan of Arc and the Hundred Years' War.
Part one. Magna Carta.
In 1215, rebel barons forced an English king to accept that even he was bound by law.
It barely lasted, but the idea became legendary.
A bad king.
King John, who ruled from 1199, lost most of England's lands in France, including Normandy in 1204, earning the nickname 'Softsword'.
To fund attempts to win them back, he squeezed his barons with heavy taxes, fees and fines, seized property, took hostages and punished enemies without trial.
He also quarrelled with the Pope over who should be Archbishop of Canterbury, and the Pope suspended most church services in England for years.
After a final defeat in France in 1214, many powerful barons had had enough.
They rebelled and captured London in 1215.
Runnymede, 1215.
In a meadow called Runnymede, beside the Thames west of London, John met the rebels and sealed a charter later divided into 63 clauses.
He didn't sign it: it was authenticated with the royal seal, and copies were sent around the kingdom.
Magna Carta means 'Great Charter' in Latin.
Most clauses dealt with barons' specific grievances: inheritance, fees, forests and fish weirs in rivers.
John agreed partly to buy time.
Within weeks he asked the Pope to cancel it, and the Pope declared it null and void.
Civil war followed.
The key promises.
Clause 39 promised that no free man would be arrested, imprisoned, stripped of property, outlawed or exiled except by the lawful judgement of his peers or by the law of the land.
Clause 40 said: 'To no one will we sell, to no one will we deny or delay right or justice.'
At the time, 'free men' excluded most people, including unfree peasants called villeins.
Other clauses were practical.
Widows kept their inheritance and couldn't be forced to remarry.
Clause 35 required standard measures for wine, ale and corn.
Most radical was clause 61: a council of 25 barons could seize the king's castles if he broke his word.
No king would accept that for long, and later versions dropped it.
It survived.
John died in 1216, and the advisers of his nine-year-old son Henry III reissued the charter in revised forms to win support, in 1216, 1217 and 1225.
Edward I confirmed it in 1297, and that version entered the statute books.
Most clauses have since been repealed, but three remain in English law, including the promise of justice and due process.
Four original copies of the 1215 charter survive, and a 1297 version, bought by the Australian government in 1952, is on display at Parliament House in Canberra.
A companion Charter of the Forest followed in 1217.
It restored ordinary people's rights to collect firewood and let pigs forage in royal forests, and said no one would lose life or limb for taking the king's deer.
It stayed on the statute books until 1971.
A myth that mattered.
In the 1600s, lawyers such as Edward Coke used Magna Carta to argue against kings claiming absolute power, and in the 1700s American colonists cited it against British rule.
Much of what they read into it, like trial by jury as we know it, went beyond what the barons intended.
Historians call this the myth of Magna Carta.
But the myth was powerful: it shaped the US Bill of Rights, and in 1948 Eleanor Roosevelt hoped the Universal Declaration of Human Rights might become an international Magna Carta.
Its deepest legacy is the rule of law: power exercised under known laws, applying even to those in charge, with a right to fair legal process.
Australia inherited this through English common law, including habeas corpus, the right to challenge unlawful detention.
The key idea: King John lost lands in France, taxed heavily and punished enemies without trial, so his barons rebelled.
Part two. Gothic cathedrals: how medieval builders made stone fly.
Without calculators or engineering degrees, medieval masons raised stone ceilings dozens of metres into the air and filled walls with glowing glass.
Here is how they pulled it off.
An abbot who wanted light.
In the 1140s Suger, abbot of Saint-Denis just north of Paris, set out to rebuild the choir of his abbey church, the burial place of French kings.
Influenced by the idea that God could be experienced as light, he wanted a church that glowed.
His builders combined existing techniques, the pointed arch, ribbed vaults and large windows, in a new way.
The result, consecrated in 1144, felt astonishingly open and bright compared with the thick-walled, shadowy Romanesque churches before it.
Historians treat it as the birth of Gothic.
The style spread through travelling master masons.
The name 'Gothic' came later, as a Renaissance insult blaming the style on the Goths.
Arches and flying buttresses.
A pointed arch pushes outwards less than a semicircular arch of the same width.
It is also adaptable: a round arch's height is fixed by its width, but a pointed one can be steeper or flatter, so narrow and wide arches reach the same height.
With ribbed vaults, a skeleton of stone ribs carrying the ceiling, masons could roof complicated spaces.
A stone vault constantly pushes the tops of the walls outwards.
Romanesque builders used thick walls and small windows.
Gothic builders moved the support outside.
A flying buttress is a half arch that leaps across the side aisle to a stone pier, catching the vault's thrust and channelling it to the ground.
Heavy pinnacles on the piers help.
The walls no longer held much up, so they became enormous windows.
Walls of coloured light.
Step inside Chartres Cathedral on a sunny day and the walls seem to dissolve into deep blues and reds.
Medieval stained glass was made by adding metal oxides to molten glass: cobalt for blue, copper for red and green.
Glaziers cut the coloured pieces, painted details such as faces and folds in dark enamel fired onto the surface, and joined everything with lead strips.
Iron frames held the panels.
The windows told Bible stories and saints' lives, and often showed the trades who paid for them, such as bakers or shoemakers.
Circular rose windows, divided like flower petals, became a signature of the style.
The deep blue of Chartres has been admired for centuries and is still hard to reproduce exactly.
Building without equations.
Medieval builders had no theory of forces in the modern sense.
Master masons worked with geometry, using compasses, set squares and string to lay out proportions, and guarded rules of thumb passed down through apprenticeships.
Designs were drawn full size on plaster floors called tracing floors, from which templates for each stone were cut.
Builders learned by trial and, sometimes, disaster.

At Beauvais in northern France, where they attempted the tallest Gothic choir of all, with a vault about forty-eight metres high, part of the vault collapsed in 1284 and was rebuilt with extra supports.
The work was also slow.
Cologne Cathedral was begun in 1248 and not finished until 1880, after centuries of interruption.
Gothic comes to Australia.
In the 1800s Gothic made a spectacular comeback.
Architects in Britain saw it as a deeply Christian and national style, and the rebuilt Houses of Parliament in London became its most famous example.
Writers found Gothic buildings romantic and mysterious, and the word lent its name to spooky novels set in crumbling castles.
It is now a neutral description.
The Revival travelled with the British Empire, and Australia is full of it.
William Wardell designed both St Mary's Cathedral in Sydney and St Patrick's Cathedral in Melbourne, with pointed arches, rib vaults and stained glass in homage to medieval models.
The main quadrangle at the University of Sydney is another well-known example.
The originals still matter: when fire tore through Notre-Dame in 2019 people worldwide watched in grief, and its reopening in December 2024 was celebrated.
The key idea: Gothic architecture began in the 1140s when Abbot Suger rebuilt Saint-Denis to glow with light.
Part three. Joan of Arc and the Hundred Years' War.
A teenage peasant girl from a village in eastern France told a prince that God had sent her to save his kingdom.
Astonishingly, she very nearly did.
A very long war.
The Hundred Years' War actually lasted 116 years, from 1337 to 1453, with long truces.
At its heart was inheritance: English kings, descended from French nobility, held lands in France and claimed the French crown itself.
England won famous victories at Crécy in 1346, Poitiers in 1356 and Agincourt in 1415, where Henry V’s outnumbered army, with its longbowmen, defeated a much larger French force.
By the 1420s, France was in desperate trouble.
The Duke of Burgundy had sided with England, and the Treaty of Troyes in 1420 declared that the English king would inherit the throne, disinheriting the French heir, Charles, known as the Dauphin.
Paris and much of the north were under English and Burgundian control.
Voices and a test.
Joan was born around 1412 in Domrémy, in north-eastern France, to a farming family.
She could not read or write.
From about thirteen, she later said, she heard voices and saw saints, especially Michael, Catherine and Margaret, who told her to go to the Dauphin, drive out the English and see him crowned.
In early 1429, at around seventeen, she persuaded a local garrison commander to give her an escort, cut her hair short and rode in men’s clothing to the Dauphin’s court at Chinon.
Charles was cautious: she could be a saint, a fraud or an agent of the devil.
Churchmen at Poitiers questioned her for weeks and found nothing wrong in her faith or conduct.
The situation was desperate enough to take a chance.
Orléans and the coronation.
Orléans, the key to southern France, had been under English siege since late 1428.
Charles gave Joan armour, a banner and a place with an army bringing supplies.
She arrived at the end of April 1429.
She did not formally command, but her presence electrified soldiers and townspeople, and she pushed for bold attacks.
She was wounded by an arrow between neck and shoulder but returned to the fight.
On 8 May the English abandoned the siege.
More victories followed, including Patay in June.
Joan then urged Charles to make the dangerous journey to Reims, the traditional site where French kings were crowned.
On 17 July 1429 he was crowned Charles VII, with Joan standing nearby holding her banner.
Captured and tried.
After the coronation, Joan’s fortunes turned.
An attack on Paris failed, and the king grew more interested in negotiation than war.
In May 1430, while defending Compiègne, she was pulled from her horse and captured by Burgundian soldiers, who sold her to the English.
There is no evidence that Charles made any serious attempt to rescue her.
In 1431 she was tried for heresy in Rouen by a Church court led by Pierre Cauchon, a bishop allied with the English.
They needed her condemned, since that would suggest Charles had been crowned with the devil’s help.
The records show an illiterate young woman answering trick questions from learned men with remarkable sharpness and courage.
Burned, then vindicated.
One major charge was that she wore men’s clothing, which her accusers treated as a sin against divine law.
Under pressure she signed a statement renouncing her claims and agreed to wear women’s dress, but days later she resumed men’s clothing, and the court declared her a relapsed heretic.
On 30 May 1431, in the market square of Rouen, she was burned at the stake.
She was about nineteen.
Within a generation, the war she had helped turn ended, as French armies took back Normandy and Gascony.
By 1453, England held only Calais.
A retrial authorised by the Pope declared the original verdict null in 1456.
Joan was made a saint in 1920 and is a patron saint of France.
The key idea: By the 1420s France was close to defeat, with English and Burgundian forces holding Paris and the north.
Quick recall. Answer out loud, or just in your head.
Question one. Why were the barons angry with King John?
Answer. He lost French lands and punished without trial.
Question two. What did Abbot Suger want his rebuilt church at Saint-Denis to achieve?
Answer. A church full of light, unlike dark Romanesque churches.
Question three. What was France’s position by the 1420s?
Answer. Close to defeat, with Paris in enemy hands.
That's the end of this episode. The questions are waiting in your review, so you can lock in what you heard.
